title: A hundred pounds of myrrh (John 19:38–42)
hook: Nicodemus, who came by night, comes by day with spices

segments.voice: Yesterday, a spear, blood and water, and a witness who insisted. Your line was he who saw it. Whose story did you listen to? Day six hundred forty-nine.

Way back in chapter three, a man came to Jesus at night. His name was Nicodemus, a Pharisee, a leader, a respected teacher. He came after dark, and he asked careful questions about being born from above, and the last we hear from him that night is a puzzled one: how can these things be? In chapter seven, he spoke up once, briefly, saying the law should give a man a hearing. And then he disappeared from the story. Now Jesus is dead. Peter, the loudest of the followers, is nowhere in this scene. And two quiet men walk forward, in daylight, to do what nobody else will.

The first is Joseph of Arimathea. John says he was a disciple, "but secretly for fear of the Jews." In John's Gospel, that phrase usually means the religious authorities, and the other Gospels say Joseph sat on their council. Now he goes to Pilate himself and asks for the body. That's a public act. Then the second man. In the King James Bible: "And there came also Nicodemus, which at the first came to Jesus by night, and brought a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about an hundred pound weight." A hundred pounds. John's pound, the Roman litra, was lighter than a modern pound, but even so, that's an enormous amount of spice. The Hebrew Bible tells of a king of Judah laid in a bed filled with spices. Some readers see Nicodemus and Joseph giving Jesus a royal burial, for the King of the Jews, as Pilate's sign said. They wrap the body in linen with the spices, as John says was the Jewish custom of burial. And there's a garden near the place of the crucifixion, and in it a new tomb where no one had ever been laid. It's close by, the Sabbath is coming, so there they lay him. Notice the arc of this man's story. He came by night in chapter three. He spoke up once in chapter seven. Now he comes by day, carrying something heavy, in front of everyone. John never tells us what Nicodemus believed in the end. Tradition makes him a saint. The text simply shows a man coming slowly into the light.
screen: then, large: `WHICH AT THE FIRST CAME TO JESUS BY NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: show your care openly. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone you care about, or a cause, or a belief, that you've kept a little quiet. Maybe you love someone and haven't said it out loud lately. Maybe you agree with someone who's being criticized and haven't said so. Maybe you've kept your faith, or your questions, to yourself. You don't have to make a speech. Just picture one small way to carry your care into the daylight. If you pray, you can ask for some of Nicodemus's courage. The bell holds the time.
A hundred pounds of myrrh. The spices Nicodemus carried in daylight, enough for a king's burial, for the man he first visited by night.
screen: `A HUNDRED POUNDS OF MYRRH — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: in daylight now. Today, take the one small step you pictured, and let your care be seen. Day six hundred forty-nine.

howItsDone: Christians remember Jesus's burial on Holy Saturday, a day of quiet waiting in many churches, and Orthodox Christians honor Joseph and Nicodemus among the myrrh-bearers on the second Sunday after Easter.

myth: Nicodemus appears only once in John's Gospel
three times: by night in chapter 3, briefly in chapter 7, and here at the burial.
the Hebrew Bible tells of a king laid in a bed of spices
King Asa, in 2 Chronicles 16:14. some readers see a royal burial in Nicodemus's hundred pounds.

he doesn't. the text shows what he did, not what he said.

fork.setup: you're Nicodemus. you once came to Jesus at night so no one would see. now he's dead, and his loud followers are hiding. what do you do?
options: bring a hundred pounds of spices and help bury him, in daylight.
send a servant with a small gift.
fork.reveal: he comes himself, openly, with myrrh and aloes, "about an hundred pound weight."

original.note: Greek: a hundred litrai, Roman pounds, each lighter than a modern pound.

trapdoor: what you thought: a lot of spices.
what it means: a royal amount, carried in daylight by a man who first came by night.
what a scholar hears: litra, the Roman pound, lighter than ours, and 2 Chronicles 16:14, a king laid in a bed of spices.

notes: 'For fear of the Jews' is quoted from KJV; the script immediately explains John's usage (the authorities) and that the other Gospels place Joseph on the council (Mark 15:43; Luke 23:50–51). Please check this is fair.
Roman litra ≈ 327 g (≈ 11.5 oz); 100 litrai ≈ 72 lb. Script says 'something like seventy-five of today's pounds'. Confirm.
2 Chronicles 16:14 (King Asa laid in a bed filled with spices). Confirm.
howItsDone: Orthodox Sunday of the Myrrh-bearers (third Sunday of Pascha counting Easter; second Sunday after Easter). Confirm wording.

Editor review (y2 pass): cut the 'seventy-five of today's pounds' / 'twelve ounces' conversion (not in the cited text); the hook no longer says Nicodemus 'went away puzzled' (John 3 records his question, not his leaving) or that the followers were 'hiding' (John says that only at 20:19); the royal-burial reading is now attributed to some readers; Joseph-on-the-council now cites Mark 15:43 and Luke 23:50–51.
